questions.q: Compute $\det\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\ 3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.expl: $2\cdot4 - 1\cdot3 = 5$.

questions.q: $A$ is a $3\times 5$ matrix. The dimension of its null space is at least:
questions.expl: rank ≤ 3, so nullity = 5 − rank ≥ 2 (rank–nullity theorem).

questions.q: The eigenvalues of an upper-triangular matrix are:
questions.expl: $\det(A-\lambda I)$ of a triangular matrix is the product of $(a_{ii}-\lambda)$.

questions.q: If $P$ is a projection matrix, then $P^2$ equals:
questions.expl: Projecting twice changes nothing: $P^2 = P$.

questions.q: Vectors $u=(1,2,-1)$ and $v=(3,-1,c)$ are orthogonal when $c$ equals:
questions.expl: $u\cdot v = 3-2-c = 0 \Rightarrow c = 1$.

questions.q: $\det(AB)$ equals:
questions.expl: Determinant is multiplicative for square matrices.

questions.q: The trace of a matrix equals:
questions.expl: Trace = sum of eigenvalues (with multiplicity); determinant is their product.

questions.q: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$, the $(1,1)$ entry of $A^{-1}$ is:
questions.expl: $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{-2}\begin{pmatrix}4&-2\\-3&1\end{pmatrix}$, so entry $= 4/(-2) = -2$.

questions.q: A set of $n$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^m$ with $n > m$ is:
opts: Dependent only if some vector is zero
questions.expl: You can't have more independent vectors than the dimension of the space.

questions.q: The column space of $A$ and the null space of $A^T$ are:
questions.expl: The four fundamental subspaces: $C(A) \perp N(A^T)$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$.

questions.q: If $Ax=b$ has no solution, least squares solves:
questions.expl: Project $b$ onto the column space: the normal equations $A^TA\hat x = A^Tb$.

questions.q: An orthogonal matrix $Q$ satisfies:
questions.expl: Orthonormal columns: $Q^TQ=I$, so $Q^{-1}=Q^T$.

questions.q: Multiplying a $3\times3$ matrix's second row by 5 multiplies its determinant by:
questions.expl: Determinant is linear in each row separately.

questions.q: Eigenvalues of $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ are:
questions.expl: Triangular matrix → eigenvalues on the diagonal.

questions.q: $A$ is diagonalizable iff:
questions.expl: Need a full eigenvector basis: $A = S\Lambda S^{-1}$. Symmetric is sufficient, not necessary; invertibility is irrelevant.

questions.q: Every real symmetric matrix has:
questions.expl: The spectral theorem: $A = Q\Lambda Q^T$.

questions.q: A matrix is positive definite iff:
questions.expl: Definition — equivalently all eigenvalues > 0, or all pivots > 0.

questions.q: Rank of $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&6\\1&1&1\end{pmatrix}$:
questions.expl: Row 2 = 2×Row 1 (dependent); rows 1 and 3 are independent.

questions.q: In the SVD $A = U\Sigma V^T$, the columns of $V$ are eigenvectors of:
questions.expl: $A^TA = V\Sigma^2V^T$; columns of $U$ are eigenvectors of $AA^T$.

questions.q: If $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of invertible $A$, then $A^{-1}$ has eigenvalue:
questions.expl: $Ax=\lambda x \Rightarrow A^{-1}x = (1/\lambda)x$.

questions.q: The dimension of the space of $3\times3$ symmetric matrices is:
questions.expl: 3 diagonal + 3 above-diagonal free entries = 6.

questions.q: Gram-Schmidt turns an independent set into:
opts: An orthonormal set with the same span
questions.expl: It orthogonalizes step by step, preserving the span — the $QR$ factorization.

questions.q: $\det(2A)$ for a $3\times3$ matrix $A$ equals:
questions.expl: Each of 3 rows is scaled: $2^3\det A = 8\det A$.

questions.q: Markov (stochastic) matrix: every column sums to 1. One eigenvalue is always:
questions.expl: $A^T\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}$, and $A$, $A^T$ share eigenvalues — steady states exist.

questions.q: Solving $Ax=0$: the special solutions correspond to:
questions.expl: One special solution per free variable; they span the null space.

questions.q: If $A$ is $4\times4$ with rank 4, then $Ax=b$:
opts: Has exactly one solution for every $b$
questions.expl: Full rank square matrix → invertible → $x=A^{-1}b$ uniquely.

questions.q: The projection of $b=(1,2)$ onto $a=(1,0)$ is:
questions.expl: $p = \frac{a^Tb}{a^Ta}a = 1\cdot(1,0)$.

questions.q: $e^{At}$ solves which equation?
questions.expl: $u(t)=e^{At}u(0)$ solves the linear ODE system.

questions.q: $A$ and $B=M^{-1}AM$ (similar matrices) always share:
questions.expl: Similarity preserves the characteristic polynomial — same eigenvalues, different eigenvectors.

questions.q: Number of pivots of a matrix equals its:
questions.expl: Pivots count independent rows/columns — the rank.

questions.q: $(AB)^T$ equals:
questions.expl: Transpose (and inverse) reverse the order of a product.

questions.q: The singular values of $A$ are:
questions.expl: $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i(A^TA)} \geq 0$.

questions.q: For the rank-1 matrix $A=uv^T$ ($u,v\neq0$), the nonzero eigenvalue is:
questions.expl: $Au = u(v^Tu)$, so $u$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $v^Tu$; the rest are 0.

questions.q: A basis for a vector space is:
questions.expl: Both properties at once; its size is the dimension.

questions.q: If all eigenvalues of $A$ satisfy $|\lambda|<1$, then $A^k$ as $k\to\infty$:
questions.expl: Powers decay like $\lambda^k$ — the stability condition for difference equations.

questions.q: $\det A \neq 0$ is equivalent to all EXCEPT:
questions.expl: Symmetry has nothing to do with invertibility.

questions.q: The pseudoinverse $A^+$ sends the column space of $A$ back to:
questions.expl: $A^+$ inverts $A$ between row space and column space, killing the null-space directions.

questions.q: Compute $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ — the second component:
In $A=LU$, the matrix $L$ records:
questions.expl: $\ell_{ij}$ = multiplier that eliminated entry $(i,j)$ — elimination run in reverse.

questions.q: The four fundamental subspaces of an $m\times n$ matrix of rank $r$: dim of the left null space is:
questions.expl: $N(A^T)\subset\mathbb{R}^m$ has dimension $m-r$.

questions.q: $\frac{d}{dx}\,x^3$ at $x=2$:
$\frac{d}{dx}\sin(x^2)$ equals:
questions.expl: Chain rule: outer $\cos$, times inner derivative $2x$.

questions.q: $\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x}$:
questions.expl: The fundamental trig limit — also the derivative of $\sin$ at 0.
$x^3/3$ from 0 to 1.

questions.q: $\frac{d}{dx}e^{3x}$ equals:
questions.expl: Chain rule with inner derivative 3.

questions.q: $\frac{d}{dx}\ln x$ equals:
questions.expl: Definition of the natural log's derivative for $x>0$.

questions.q: The derivative of $f(x)=x\,e^x$ is:
questions.expl: Product rule: $1\cdot e^x + x\cdot e^x$.

questions.q: $f'(c)=0$ and $f''(c)<0$ means $c$ is a local:
questions.expl: Second derivative test: concave down at a critical point → max.

questions.q: $\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{3x^2+x}{x^2-5}$:
questions.expl: Leading terms dominate: $3x^2/x^2 = 3$.

questions.q: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says $\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ equals:
questions.expl: Differentiation undoes integration — FTC part 1.

questions.q: $\int \frac{1}{x}\,dx$ equals:
questions.expl: The antiderivative of $1/x$; absolute value covers $x<0$.

questions.q: $\int_0^{\pi}\sin x\,dx$:
Linear approximation of $\sqrt{1+x}$ near $x=0$:
questions.expl: $f(0)=1$, $f'(0)=\tfrac12$ → $1+x/2$. The most-used approximation in physics.

questions.q: $\frac{d}{dx}\tan x$ equals:
questions.expl: Quotient rule on $\sin/\cos$ gives $1/\cos^2 = \sec^2$.

questions.q: If $y^2 + x^2 = 25$, then $\frac{dy}{dx}$ equals:
questions.expl: Implicit differentiation: $2x + 2y\,y' = 0$.

questions.q: $\int x e^{x}\,dx$ equals:
questions.expl: Integration by parts: $uv - \int v\,du = xe^x - e^x$.

questions.q: Taylor series of $e^x$ at 0 starts:
questions.expl: $\sum x^n/n!$ — the factorials are the signature.

questions.q: $\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{e^x - 1 - x}{x^2}$:
questions.expl: From the series $e^x = 1+x+x^2/2+\dots$, or L'Hôpital twice.

questions.q: Average value of $f(x)=x$ on $[0,4]$:
A critical point of $f(x)=x^3-3x$ occurs at $x=1$. It is a local:
questions.expl: $f''(x)=6x>0$ at $x=1$ → minimum.

questions.q: $\frac{d}{dx}\arctan x$ equals:
questions.expl: Inverse function differentiation — memorize this one; it appears everywhere.

questions.q: $\int_1^e \frac{1}{x}\,dx$:
Volume of the solid: $y=\sqrt{x}$, $0\le x\le 4$ rotated about the x-axis:
questions.expl: Disks: $\pi\int_0^4 x\,dx = 8\pi$.

questions.q: L'Hôpital's rule applies directly to:
questions.expl: Indeterminate quotients only; other forms must be rewritten first.

questions.q: $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} r^n$ converges to $\frac{1}{1-r}$ when:
questions.expl: Geometric series convergence condition.

questions.q: $\frac{d}{dx}[f(g(x))]$ equals:
questions.expl: The chain rule — the single most important formula for deep learning (backprop IS this).

questions.q: $\int_0^{\infty} e^{-x}\,dx$:
questions.expl: $[-e^{-x}]_0^{\infty} = 0-(-1) = 1$. Improper but convergent.

questions.q: Newton's method iterates $x_{n+1} =$
questions.expl: Follow the tangent line to its root — gradient descent's ancestor.

questions.q: $\frac{d}{dx}x^x$ equals:
questions.expl: Logarithmic differentiation: $y=e^{x\ln x}$, $y'=x^x(\ln x+1)$.

questions.q: Arc length of $y=f(x)$ on $[a,b]$:
questions.expl: Pythagoras on infinitesimal pieces: $\sqrt{dx^2+dy^2}$.

questions.q: If $f'(x) > 0$ on an interval, $f$ is:
questions.expl: Sign of $f'$ controls monotonicity; concavity is $f''$.

questions.q: $\int \cos^2 x\,dx$ uses which identity?
questions.expl: Half-angle identity turns it into an easy integral: $\tfrac{x}{2}+\tfrac{\sin 2x}{4}+C$.

questions.q: $\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$ is the definition of:
questions.expl: The difference quotient — where everything begins.

questions.q: The Taylor series of $\sin x$ contains only:
questions.expl: $x - x^3/3! + x^5/5! - \dots$ — $\sin$ is odd.

questions.q: Separation of variables solves $\frac{dy}{dx}=ky$ giving:
questions.expl: Exponential growth/decay — the most important ODE in existence.

questions.q: The Mean Value Theorem guarantees a $c$ with:
questions.expl: Somewhere the instantaneous rate equals the average rate (for differentiable $f$).

questions.q: $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2y + y^3)$ equals:
questions.expl: Treat $y$ as constant — your first partial derivative, the door to gradients.

questions.q: $\int \frac{2x}{x^2+1}\,dx$ equals:
questions.expl: $u$-substitution with $u=x^2+1$: numerator is exactly $du$.

questions.q: $e^{i\pi}+1$ equals:
questions.expl: Euler's identity — the five great constants in one line. You'll meet $e^{i\theta}$ again in Fourier transforms.

questions.q: How many ways to arrange 5 distinct books on a shelf?
$\binom{10}{3}$ equals:
questions.expl: $\frac{10\cdot9\cdot8}{3\cdot2\cdot1}=120$.

questions.q: Two fair dice: $P(\text{sum}=7)$ equals:
questions.expl: 6 favorable outcomes out of 36.

questions.q: $P(A\cup B)$ equals:
questions.expl: Inclusion–exclusion; adding double-counts the overlap.

questions.q: Bayes' rule: $P(A\mid B)$ equals:
questions.expl: The theorem underneath every spam filter, diagnostic test, and LLM evaluation.

questions.q: A test is 99% accurate; the disease affects 1 in 1000. Given a positive test, $P(\text{disease})$ is roughly:
questions.expl: Base rates dominate: $\frac{0.99\cdot0.001}{0.99\cdot0.001+0.01\cdot0.999}\approx 0.09$. The most famous Bayes trap.

questions.q: $A$ and $B$ independent means:
questions.expl: Disjoint (mutually exclusive) is NOT independence — disjoint events are maximally dependent.

questions.q: In the Monty Hall problem, switching wins with probability:
questions.expl: Your first pick wins $\tfrac13$ of the time; switching wins whenever the first pick was wrong.

questions.q: $X\sim\text{Bin}(n,p)$. $E[X]$ equals:
questions.expl: Linearity of expectation over $n$ indicator variables — the mighty indicator trick.

questions.q: $X\sim\text{Bin}(n,p)$. $\text{Var}(X)$ equals:
questions.expl: Sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli variances.

questions.q: Roll a fair die. $E[X]$ equals:
Linearity of expectation $E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]$ requires:
questions.expl: The superpower: it holds even for dependent variables.

questions.q: $X\sim\text{Pois}(\lambda)$. $E[X]$ and $\text{Var}(X)$ are:
questions.expl: The Poisson's signature: mean = variance = $\lambda$.

questions.q: The Poisson approximates the Binomial when:
questions.expl: The law of rare events, with $\lambda = np$.

questions.q: For a continuous random variable, $P(X = c)$ for any exact point $c$ is:
questions.expl: Probability lives in intervals (areas under the density), not points.

questions.q: A PDF $f(x)$ must satisfy:
questions.expl: Densities can exceed 1 (e.g. Uniform(0, ½)); the area is what must be 1.

questions.q: $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Approximately $P(-2\le Z\le 2)$ is:
questions.expl: The 68–95–99.7 rule at 2 standard deviations.

questions.q: $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$; then $aX+b$ is distributed:
questions.expl: Normality survives linear maps — location scales by $a$, adds $b$; variance by $a^2$.

questions.q: The exponential distribution is the only continuous one that is:
questions.expl: $P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t)$ — a fresh start at every moment.

questions.q: $X\sim\text{Expo}(\lambda)$. $E[X]$ equals:
questions.expl: Rate $\lambda$ events per unit time → mean wait $1/\lambda$.

questions.q: LOTUS computes $E[g(X)]$ as:
questions.expl: Law of the Unconscious Statistician — no need to find $g(X)$'s distribution first.

questions.q: $E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$ equals:
questions.expl: The fundamental variance identity.

questions.q: Is $E[X^2] \geq (E[X])^2$ always true?
questions.expl: It IS the statement $\text{Var}(X)\ge0$ (also Jensen's inequality for $x^2$).

questions.q: $\text{Cov}(X,Y)=0$ implies $X,Y$ independent:
questions.expl: Uncorrelated ≠ independent in general ($X$, $X^2$ with symmetric $X$) — but for multivariate normals it does.

questions.q: Correlation is always in:
questions.expl: Cauchy–Schwarz bounds it; ±1 means a perfect linear relationship.

questions.q: $\text{Var}(X+Y)$ for independent $X,Y$:
questions.expl: Covariance term vanishes under independence. Standard deviations do NOT add.

questions.q: The Central Limit Theorem says the sum of many iid variables approaches:
questions.expl: Regardless of the original distribution (finite variance) — why the normal is everywhere.

questions.q: The Law of Large Numbers says the sample mean converges to:
questions.expl: LLN gives the destination; CLT describes the fluctuations around it.

questions.q: First success on trial $k$ with probability $p$ each — $P(X=k)$ is:
questions.expl: Geometric: $k-1$ failures then a success.

questions.q: Expected number of flips of a fair coin to see the first heads:
questions.expl: Geometric mean $1/p = 2$.

questions.q: 10 people, expected number of shared-birthday pairs among $\binom{10}{2}=45$ pairs:
questions.expl: Indicators + linearity: each pair matches with prob $1/365$.

questions.q: A fair coin flipped 5 times: $P(\text{exactly 3 heads})$ equals:
The MGF $M(t)=E[e^{tX}]$ is useful because:
opts: Its derivatives at 0 give the moments
questions.expl: $M^{(n)}(0) = E[X^n]$; MGFs also uniquely determine distributions and tame sums.

questions.q: $X\sim\text{Unif}(0,1)$. $E[X^2]$ equals:
questions.expl: LOTUS: $\int_0^1 x^2dx = \tfrac13$ (so Var $= \tfrac13-\tfrac14=\tfrac1{12}$).

questions.q: Conditional expectation $E[Y\mid X]$ is:
questions.expl: It's the best predictor of $Y$ given $X$ — the concept beneath regression and much of ML.

questions.q: Adam's law (tower property): $E[E[Y\mid X]]$ equals:
questions.expl: Iterated expectation — condition, then average over what you conditioned on.

questions.q: Markov's inequality: for $X\ge0$, $P(X\ge a)$ is at most:
questions.expl: The crudest but most general tail bound; Chebyshev refines it with variance.

questions.q: A Markov chain's next state depends on:
questions.expl: The Markov property — the foundation of MDPs and reinforcement learning.

questions.q: A stationary distribution $\pi$ of chain $P$ satisfies:
questions.expl: Left eigenvector with eigenvalue 1 — probability's meeting point with linear algebra (and PageRank).

questions.q: Sample two cards without replacement. $P(\text{both aces})$ equals:
questions.expl: Multiplication rule with updated conditioning — without replacement changes the second factor.

questions.q: Backpropagation is, at its mathematical core:
opts: The chain rule applied recursively through a computation graph
questions.expl: Every deep learning framework is chain rule + bookkeeping.

questions.q: In micrograd, each Value node stores data and:
opts: Its gradient and a backward closure
questions.expl: grad accumulates ∂L/∂node; _backward knows the local chain-rule step.

questions.q: The gradient of $L$ with respect to a weight tells you:
opts: How much $L$ changes per unit nudge of that weight
questions.expl: A local linear sensitivity — the direction to nudge to reduce loss.

questions.q: Gradient descent updates weights by:
questions.expl: Step against the gradient, scaled by learning rate $\eta$.

questions.q: Why is the gradient zeroed before each backward pass?
questions.expl: Forgetting zero_grad() is the classic bug — stale gradients add up.

questions.q: In a backward pass through addition $c = a + b$, the gradient flowing to $a$ is:
questions.expl: Addition routes gradients equally; multiplication swaps in the other operand.

questions.q: For $c = a\cdot b$, $\frac{\partial c}{\partial a}$ equals:
questions.expl: Local derivative of a product w.r.t. one factor is the other factor.

questions.q: $\tanh$ saturation is a problem because:
opts: Its gradient goes to ~0, killing learning for that neuron
questions.expl: Flat regions → vanishing gradients — the diagnosis at the heart of makemore 3.

questions.q: Softmax converts logits into:
questions.expl: $e^{z_i}/\sum_j e^{z_j}$ — the output layer of every classifier and LLM.

questions.q: Cross-entropy loss for the correct class with predicted probability $p$:
questions.expl: Negative log-likelihood: confident-and-wrong is punished brutally.

questions.q: A bigram character model predicts the next character using:
questions.expl: The simplest possible language model — makemore's starting point.

questions.q: Why can a count-based bigram model and a 1-layer neural net give identical results?
opts: The net's optimum recovers the (log) count ratios
questions.expl: Gradient descent on NLL converges to the same conditional probabilities as normalized counts.

questions.q: An embedding layer is effectively:
opts: A learned lookup table mapping tokens to vectors
questions.expl: Index into a trainable matrix — tokens become geometry.

questions.q: Train / dev / test splits exist to:
opts: Measure generalization and tune without contaminating the final estimate
questions.expl: Tune on dev; touch test rarely — else you overfit your decisions to it.

questions.q: If training loss ≪ validation loss, the model is:
questions.expl: Memorizing specifics that don't generalize — regularize, get data, or shrink.

questions.q: Minibatching trades:
opts: Gradient exactness for speed (noisy but frequent updates)
questions.expl: Noisy estimates are cheap; the noise even helps escape bad regions.

questions.q: A good initial learning rate is often found by:
opts: An LR sweep — try a range, plot loss vs. LR
questions.expl: Exactly what Karpathy does in makemore 2 — sweep, then decay late in training.

questions.q: With bad initialization, initial loss is far above $-\log(1/\text{vocab})$. That baseline is the loss of:
questions.expl: Sanity-check trick: know what loss 'knowing nothing' gives before training.

questions.q: BatchNorm normalizes:
opts: Each feature over the batch to zero mean, unit variance (then scales/shifts)
The inputs only at test time
questions.expl: Stabilizes activation distributions; gain/bias restore expressiveness.

questions.q: Why does BatchNorm behave differently at inference?
opts: It uses running mean/var instead of batch statistics
questions.expl: No batch to average over — hence the running estimates (and many subtle bugs).

questions.q: 'Dead neurons' are units that:
opts: Never activate for any input, so their gradients are always ~0
questions.expl: E.g. a saturated tanh or a ReLU pushed permanently negative — initialization matters.

questions.q: Kaiming/He-style initialization scales weights by roughly:
questions.expl: Keeps activation variance stable layer to layer — the fix explored in makemore 3.

questions.q: The residual (skip) connection computes:
questions.expl: A gradient superhighway — deep transformers are trainable because of it.

questions.q: In self-attention, each token computes attention weights via:
opts: Dot products between its query and all keys, then softmax
questions.expl: $\text{softmax}(QK^T/\sqrt{d_k})V$ — data-dependent, learned communication.

questions.q: The $\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling in attention prevents:
opts: Softmax saturation from large dot products
questions.expl: Large-variance logits → peaky softmax → tiny gradients. Scale keeps variance ~1.

questions.q: Causal (masked) attention means a token attends to:
questions.expl: The autoregressive mask: you may not look at the future you're predicting.

questions.q: The 'heads' in multi-head attention are:
opts: Parallel attention subspaces, concatenated then projected
questions.expl: Several smaller attentions attend to different relationship types simultaneously.

questions.q: A transformer block is (in order, GPT-style):
opts: LayerNorm → attention → residual → LayerNorm → MLP → residual
questions.expl: Communicate (attention) then compute (MLP), each wrapped in pre-norm + residual.

questions.q: Positional information is needed because attention alone is:
opts: Permutation-invariant — it has no idea of order
questions.expl: Without position embeddings, 'dog bites man' = 'man bites dog'.

questions.q: LayerNorm differs from BatchNorm by normalizing over:
questions.expl: No batch statistics → same behavior train/test — why transformers prefer it.

questions.q: Byte-pair encoding (BPE) builds a vocabulary by:
opts: Repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair
questions.expl: Greedy merges — the algorithm you implement in the tokenizer video.

questions.q: Why can LLMs struggle to spell words or reverse strings?
opts: Tokenization: they see chunks, not characters
questions.expl: 'strawberry' may be 2–3 opaque tokens — half of LLM weirdness is tokenization.

questions.q: Sampling with temperature $T > 1$ makes generations:
questions.expl: Logits divided by $T$ flatten the distribution; $T\to0$ approaches argmax.

questions.q: Perplexity is:
opts: The exponential of the average negative log-likelihood
questions.expl: Effective branching factor — how 'surprised' the model is per token.

questions.q: Pretraining vs. finetuning:
opts: Next-token prediction on huge corpora, then adaptation on smaller targeted data
questions.expl: The two-stage recipe behind every modern assistant (plus RLHF/DPO on top).

questions.q: Mixed-precision training (bf16/fp16) mainly buys:
opts: Speed and memory savings with minimal accuracy cost
questions.expl: Key ingredient in the GPT-2 reproduction video — hardware-aware training.

questions.q: Gradient clipping protects against:
questions.expl: Cap the global norm so one bad batch can't launch the weights into orbit.

questions.q: In 'backprop ninja' you verify manual gradients by:
opts: Comparing your tensors against PyTorch autograd element-wise
questions.expl: cmp() against autograd — exact agreement or you found a bug.

questions.q: Weight decay (L2 regularization) pushes weights toward:
questions.expl: Adds $\lambda\|w\|^2$ to the loss — smaller weights, smoother functions.

questions.q: The dominant FLOPs in a transformer forward pass come from:
questions.expl: Attention + MLP matmuls — why GPUs (matmul machines) rule AI, and why CS 150 + GPU work matter.

questions.q: Average-case lookup in a hash map is:
questions.expl: Hash → bucket directly; worst case degrades with collisions.

questions.q: Binary search requires the input to be:
opts: A power of two in length
questions.expl: Halving only works if order tells you which half to keep.

questions.q: Binary search on $n$ elements runs in:
questions.expl: Each step halves the search space.

questions.q: Two Sum in $O(n)$ uses:
opts: A hash map of seen values
questions.expl: For each x, check if target − x was already seen.

questions.q: The two-pointer technique typically applies when the array is:
opts: Sorted (or you control movement by a monotonic condition)
questions.expl: Pointer moves must be justified by monotonicity — that's the whole trick.

questions.q: Sliding window is the right tool for:
opts: Contiguous subarray/substring problems with a shrink/grow condition
questions.expl: Grow the right edge, shrink the left when the invariant breaks.

questions.q: Valid Parentheses is solved with:
questions.expl: Push opens; on a close, the top must match — LIFO mirrors nesting.

questions.q: A queue serves elements in:
questions.expl: First in, first out — BFS's data structure.

questions.q: Quicksort's average and worst cases:
questions.expl: Bad pivots (already-sorted input, naive pivot) degrade it; randomization protects.

questions.q: Merge sort's time and extra space:
questions.expl: Stable and predictable — the merge step costs the linear buffer.

questions.q: A min-heap gives you which operation in $O(1)$?
questions.expl: Root is the min; insert/extract are $O(\log n)$; arbitrary search is $O(n)$.

questions.q: Top-K frequent elements is classically solved with:
opts: A heap of size K (or bucket sort)
questions.expl: $O(n\log k)$ with a bounded heap; bucket-by-count achieves $O(n)$.

questions.q: Detecting a cycle in a linked list uses:
questions.expl: If there's a loop, the hare laps the tortoise.

questions.q: Reversing a singly linked list iteratively needs how much extra space?
questions.expl: Three pointers: prev, curr, next — rewire as you walk.

questions.q: In-order traversal of a binary search tree visits nodes in:
questions.expl: Left–root–right + BST property = ascending sequence. Key to 'Kth smallest'.

questions.q: BFS on a tree processes nodes:
opts: Level by level, using a queue
questions.expl: Exactly what 'Level Order Traversal' asks for.

questions.q: DFS's natural implementations are:
questions.expl: The call stack IS the stack; iterative DFS makes it explicit.

questions.q: Number of Islands is at heart:
questions.expl: Each unvisited land cell starts a new component; sink it as you explore.

questions.q: Course Schedule (can you finish all courses?) is:
opts: Cycle detection in a directed graph / topological sort
questions.expl: Prerequisites form a DAG iff no cycle — Kahn's algorithm or DFS colors.

questions.q: Dijkstra's algorithm fails when:
questions.expl: Greedy settlement assumes no future shortcut — negative edges break that (use Bellman-Ford).

questions.q: A trie excels at:
questions.expl: One node per character; shared prefixes shared once — Word Search II's weapon.

questions.q: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has:
questions.expl: Memoize repeated subproblems; build optimal answers from optimal parts.

questions.q: Climbing Stairs (1 or 2 steps) counts paths via:
questions.expl: Last move was a 1-step or a 2-step — sum both histories.

questions.q: Coin Change (fewest coins) is naturally:
questions.expl: Greedy fails for coins like {1,3,4} making 6 — DP considers all last-coin choices.

questions.q: Kadane's algorithm (Maximum Subarray) keeps:
opts: Best sum ending at the current index, resetting when it goes negative
questions.expl: A negative running sum can never help the future — drop it. $O(n)$.

questions.q: Backtracking generates subsets/permutations by:
questions.expl: DFS over decisions, undoing state on the way back up.

questions.q: Merging overlapping intervals starts with:
questions.expl: After sorting, overlap checks are only ever against the last merged interval.

questions.q: Amortized $O(1)$ append in dynamic arrays comes from:
opts: Doubling capacity so copies are rare
questions.expl: Occasional $O(n)$ copies averaged over $n$ appends = constant per append.

questions.q: $n$ XOR $n$ equals, and $n$ XOR $0$ equals:
questions.expl: The two identities behind Single Number and Missing Number.

questions.q: An LRU cache in $O(1)$ per operation combines:
questions.expl: Map gives lookup; the list reorders recency and evicts the tail in constant time.

questions.q: For $f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, what is the shape of the gradient $\nabla f$?
questions.expl: A scalar-valued function of $n$ inputs has one partial derivative per input — an $n$-vector. This shape discipline is the core skill of matrix calculus.

questions.q: For $f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$, the Jacobian $J$ has shape:
questions.expl: One row per output, one column per input: $J_{ij} = \partial f_i / \partial x_j$, so $m \times n$.

questions.q: $\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(x^T A x\right) = $
questions.expl: In general $(A+A^T)x$; it collapses to $2Ax$ only when $A$ is symmetric. Deep learning losses usually involve symmetric forms, which is why you often see $2Ax$.

questions.q: For the linear map $f(x) = Ax$, the Jacobian is:
questions.expl: A linear map is its own best linear approximation — the Jacobian of $Ax$ is exactly $A$.

questions.q: Chain rule with shapes: $g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$, $f:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}$, $h = f \circ g$. Then $\nabla h(x) =$
questions.expl: $J_g^T$ is $n \times m$ and $\nabla f$ is $m$-dimensional, giving an $n$-vector. Backpropagation is exactly this: transpose-Jacobian times upstream gradient.

questions.q: $\dfrac{\partial}{\partial A}\,\mathrm{tr}(AB) = $
questions.expl: $\mathrm{tr}(AB) = \sum_{ij} A_{ij}B_{ji}$, so $\partial/\partial A_{ij} = B_{ji}$ — i.e. $B^T$. Trace identities are the workhorse of matrix gradient derivations.

questions.q: Jacobi's formula: for invertible $A$, $\dfrac{\partial \det A}{\partial A} = $
questions.expl: $d(\det A) = \det(A)\,\mathrm{tr}(A^{-1} dA)$, which as a gradient reads $\det(A) A^{-T}$. This appears in normalizing flows and log-det terms.

questions.q: $f(x, y) = x^2 y + 3y$. Compute $\partial f / \partial y$ at $(x,y) = (2, 1)$.
questions.expl: $\partial f/\partial y = x^2 + 3 = 4 + 3 = 7$. Partials treat the other variables as constants.

questions.q: The Hessian of a twice continuously differentiable $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ is:
questions.expl: Schwarz's theorem: mixed partials commute, so $H_{ij} = H_{ji}$. Positive definiteness only holds at strict local minima.

questions.q: $\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \|x\|_2^2 = $
questions.expl: $\|x\|^2 = x^T x$, and the quadratic-form rule with $A = I$ gives $2x$. The single most-used gradient in ML.

questions.q: Reverse-mode automatic differentiation (backprop) is preferred in deep learning because:
opts: It is numerically more accurate than forward mode
One backward pass gives the gradient w.r.t. ALL inputs when the output is a scalar loss
It uses less memory than forward mode
questions.expl: Reverse mode costs one pass per OUTPUT; training has one scalar loss and millions of parameters, so one backward pass beats millions of forward-mode passes. The price is storing activations — hence more memory, not less.

questions.q: Forward-mode autodiff via dual numbers computes, in one pass:
questions.expl: Each forward pass propagates one tangent vector — a JVP. Full Jacobians need one pass per input dimension, which is why forward mode suits few-input problems.

questions.q: The gradient descent update with learning rate $\eta$ is:
questions.expl: Step against the gradient — the direction of steepest local decrease.

questions.q: $f(x) = x^2$, starting at $x_0 = 3$ with $\eta = 0.1$. After one gradient step, $x_1 = $
For a convex function, every local minimum is:
questions.expl: Convexity's superpower: the bowl has no false valleys. (The minimum need not be unique — think of a flat-bottomed bowl.)

questions.q: Momentum helps gradient descent primarily by:
opts: Accumulating a running average of gradients, damping oscillation across steep directions while accelerating along consistent ones
Guaranteeing convergence to a global minimum
questions.expl: In a ravine, plain GD zig-zags across the walls; momentum's exponential average cancels the zig-zag components and builds speed along the valley floor.

questions.q: Adam differs from SGD-with-momentum by additionally:
opts: Scaling each parameter's step by a running estimate of the gradient's second moment (per-parameter adaptive step sizes)
Removing the need for a learning rate
questions.expl: Adam keeps both a first-moment (momentum) and second-moment estimate; dividing by $\sqrt{\hat v}$ gives each parameter its own effective step size.

questions.q: Adam's bias correction ($\hat m = m / (1 - \beta_1^t)$) exists because:
opts: The moment estimates start at zero and are underestimated in early steps
questions.expl: With $m_0 = 0$, the exponential average needs several steps to warm up; dividing by $1-\beta^t$ exactly cancels that startup bias.

questions.q: A learning rate that is clearly too high typically produces:
opts: A loss that oscillates or diverges
questions.expl: Steps overshoot the minimum and bounce or explode. The classic first diagnostic when loss goes to NaN.

questions.q: In high-dimensional deep learning loss landscapes, the dominant obstacle is believed to be:
opts: Saddle points and plateaus rather than bad local minima
questions.expl: In high dimensions a critical point needs every direction to curve upward to be a true minimum — overwhelmingly unlikely; most critical points are saddles.

questions.q: Weight decay corresponds to:
opts: Shrinking weights toward zero each step (an $L_2$-style penalty; decoupled from the gradient in AdamW)
questions.expl: Each update multiplies weights by $(1 - \eta\lambda)$. AdamW's insight: apply it directly rather than through Adam's adaptive scaling.

questions.q: Learning-rate warmup followed by cosine decay is used because:
opts: It maximizes the final learning rate
Early optimizer statistics are noisy — a small initial rate avoids instability, then a smooth decay lets training settle into a sharp minimum
It is required for convergence proofs
questions.expl: Warmup protects the fragile early phase (especially with Adam's untrustworthy early second moments); cosine decay anneals steps so the model can settle.

questions.q: The entropy of a fair coin flip, in bits:
questions.expl: $H = -\left(\tfrac12\log_2\tfrac12 + \tfrac12\log_2\tfrac12\right) = 1$ bit — the unit itself is defined by this case.

questions.q: The entropy of a uniform distribution over 8 outcomes, in bits:
questions.expl: $H = \log_2 8 = 3$. Uniform distributions maximize entropy — total uncertainty, three yes/no questions to pin down.

questions.q: Shannon entropy is defined as:
questions.expl: The expected surprise $-\log p(x)$. Rare events carry more information; entropy is the average.

questions.q: Which is TRUE of KL divergence $D_{KL}(p \| q)$?
opts: It can be negative for continuous distributions
questions.expl: Gibbs' inequality gives non-negativity with equality iff the distributions match. It is NOT symmetric — $D_{KL}(p\|q) \neq D_{KL}(q\|p)$ — which is why it isn't a metric.

questions.q: Cross-entropy decomposes as $H(p, q) = $
questions.expl: Since $H(p)$ is fixed by the data, minimizing cross-entropy in $q$ is exactly minimizing $D_{KL}(p\|q)$ — this is why cross-entropy is THE loss for classification and language modeling.

questions.q: Training a language model by minimizing negative log-likelihood is equivalent to:
opts: Minimizing the cross-entropy between the empirical data distribution and the model
Minimizing the model's perplexity on the training set — both this and the cross-entropy statement
Minimizing KL from the model to a uniform prior
questions.expl: NLL = cross-entropy against the empirical distribution, and perplexity is just $e^{\text{NLL}}$ — three names for one objective.

questions.q: Mutual information $I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y)$ equals zero exactly when:
questions.expl: Knowing $Y$ reduces uncertainty about $X$ by $I(X;Y)$ bits; independence means knowing $Y$ tells you nothing.

questions.q: Shannon's source coding theorem says:
opts: Any data can be compressed to arbitrary size
Lossless compression cannot beat the entropy of the source (in bits per symbol, on average)
Entropy limits only apply to text
questions.expl: Entropy is the hard floor for lossless compression. Deep connection to LLMs: a better language model IS a better compressor of text.

questions.q: In "Attention Is All You Need", scores are computed as $\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}$. Why divide by $\sqrt{d_k}$?
opts: To normalize the output to unit length
Dot products grow with dimension, pushing softmax into saturated regions with tiny gradients
questions.expl: For random $d_k$-dimensional vectors the dot product has variance $\propto d_k$; dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps logits in softmax's sensitive range.

questions.q: ResNet's core contribution was:
opts: Skip connections that let layers learn residuals, keeping very deep networks trainable
questions.expl: Identity shortcuts give gradients a direct highway and reframe each block as learning a correction — the fix for the degradation problem in very deep nets.

questions.q: Chinchilla's headline finding:
opts: Compute-optimal training uses roughly 20 tokens per parameter — most LLMs of the time were undertrained on data
questions.expl: For a fixed compute budget, model size and training tokens should scale together (~20:1 tokens:params). Gopher-sized models were data-starved; Chinchilla beat them at a quarter of the size.

questions.q: LoRA finetunes a frozen weight matrix $W$ by learning:
opts: A low-rank update $\Delta W = BA$ with rank $r \ll d$, training only $A$ and $B$
questions.expl: Two thin matrices carry the task-specific update — under 1% of parameters, tiny optimizer state, and adapters you can hot-swap over one base model.

questions.q: DPO's improvement over the RLHF pipeline is:
opts: Deriving a closed-form loss on preference pairs, removing the separate reward model and the RL loop entirely
Human labels are no longer needed
questions.expl: DPO's key move: the RLHF objective has an analytic solution, so preference data can train the policy directly with a simple classification-style loss.

questions.q: ViT processes an image by:
opts: Splitting it into fixed-size patches, embedding each, and running a standard transformer over the patch sequence
Processing raw pixels row by row with an RNN
questions.expl: "An image is worth 16×16 words" — patches are tokens. With enough data, the transformer matches or beats CNN inductive biases.

questions.q: CLIP is trained with:
opts: A contrastive objective aligning matching image–text pairs and repelling mismatched ones across a batch
questions.expl: Two encoders, one shared embedding space — which is what makes zero-shot classification possible: classify by comparing to text prompts.

questions.q: BERT vs GPT pretraining:
opts: BERT uses bidirectional masked-token prediction; GPT predicts the next token left-to-right
BERT is autoregressive; GPT is not
questions.expl: Masked LM sees both sides of context — great for understanding tasks; causal LM can generate. The generative path won the scaling race.

questions.q: The InstructGPT pipeline, in order:
opts: Supervised finetuning → train a reward model on human preference rankings → optimize the policy with PPO
questions.expl: SFT teaches the format, the reward model captures human preference, PPO pushes the policy toward it (with a KL leash to stay close to SFT).

questions.q: DDPM trains a network to:
opts: Generate images in one forward pass
Predict the noise added at each step of a gradual noising process, so sampling can reverse it
questions.expl: Forward: destroy data with scheduled Gaussian noise. Learned reverse: denoise step by step. The simplified objective is just MSE on the predicted noise.

questions.q: FlashAttention achieves exact attention with less memory by:
opts: Approximating softmax with a kernel trick
Tiling Q/K/V through fast on-chip SRAM and computing softmax online, never materializing the $N \times N$ score matrix
questions.expl: It's an IO-aware reordering of the same math — memory drops from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N)$ and it's FASTER because HBM traffic, not FLOPs, was the bottleneck.

questions.q: In a Mixtral-style MoE layer, "active" vs "total" parameters means:
opts: Nothing — all parameters are always used
A router sends each token to $k$ of $N$ expert MLPs, so per-token compute uses only the chosen experts while ALL experts must sit in memory
questions.expl: Mixtral 8x7B: ~47B total, ~13B active per token (top-2 of 8). Compute scales with active; memory scales with total — the MoE tradeoff in one line.

questions.q: A 7B-parameter model stored in bf16 (2 bytes/param) needs approximately how many GB for weights alone?
questions.expl: $7\text{B} \times 2$ bytes $= 14$ GB. The first number to compute before renting any GPU.

questions.q: GPT-2 small (124M parameters) in fp32 (4 bytes/param) needs approximately how many MB for weights?
questions.expl: $124\text{M} \times 4 = 496$ MB. Weights alone — training multiplies this several times over.

questions.q: Full finetuning with Adam in mixed precision needs roughly how much memory relative to bf16 weights alone?
opts: Roughly 6–8× (weights + gradients + fp32 master weights and two Adam moments)
questions.expl: Per parameter: bf16 weight (2B) + bf16 grad (2B) + fp32 master (4B) + two fp32 Adam states (8B) ≈ 16 bytes vs 2 — why a 7B full finetune laughs at a 24GB card, and why LoRA/ZeRO exist.

questions.q: KV-cache size per token $\approx 2 \times n_{layers} \times d_{model} \times$ bytes. For 32 layers, $d_{model} = 4096$, bf16 (2 bytes): how many MB per token?
questions.expl: $2 \cdot 32 \cdot 4096 \cdot 2 = 524{,}288$ bytes $= 0.5$ MB per token — a 4k-token context holds ~2 GB of cache. This is what PagedAttention and GQA fight.

questions.q: Self-attention compute scales with sequence length $N$ as:
questions.expl: Every token attends to every other. Long-context work is a war against this quadratic.

questions.q: Average cross-entropy loss of 2.079 nats per token corresponds to a perplexity of approximately:
questions.expl: Perplexity $= e^{2.079} \approx 8$ — the model is 'as confused as' a uniform choice among 8 tokens. Report the loss's exponential, always.

questions.q: Gradient checkpointing trades:
opts: Extra recomputation in the backward pass (~1 extra forward) for large activation-memory savings
questions.expl: Store only checkpoint activations, recompute the rest during backward — roughly 30% more compute for dramatically less memory.

questions.q: Data parallelism vs tensor parallelism:
opts: Data parallel replicates the model and splits the batch; tensor parallel splits individual weight matrices across devices
Tensor parallel only works at inference
questions.expl: DP syncs gradients once per step (all-reduce); TP communicates inside every layer — which is why TP wants NVLink-class bandwidth and DP tolerates slower links.

questions.q: RoPE (rotary position embeddings) encodes position by:
opts: Adding a learned vector per position
Rotating query/key vectors by position-dependent angles so their dot product depends on RELATIVE position
questions.expl: Rotation makes $q_m \cdot k_n$ a function of $m - n$ — relative offsets fall out of the geometry. Used by LLaMA and nearly every modern open model.

questions.q: BPE tokenization builds its vocabulary by:
opts: Iteratively merging the most frequent adjacent symbol pairs until the vocab budget is reached
Using a fixed dictionary of English words
questions.expl: Frequent strings become single tokens, rare ones decompose into pieces — no out-of-vocabulary tokens, adjustable granularity. You'll build this from scratch in the tokenizer lab.

questions.q: Sampling temperature $T$ works by:
opts: Dividing logits by $T$ before softmax — $T \to 0$ approaches greedy decoding, $T > 1$ flattens the distribution
questions.expl: Temperature reshapes confidence: low sharpens (deterministic, repetitive), high flattens (creative, error-prone).

questions.q: Top-p (nucleus) sampling:
opts: Samples from the smallest token set whose cumulative probability exceeds $p$
Picks the single most likely token with probability $p$
questions.expl: The candidate set adapts to the model's confidence — narrow when it's sure, wide when it's not. Usually combined with temperature.

questions.q: Benchmark contamination means:
opts: Test data leaked into the pretraining corpus, inflating scores without real capability
questions.expl: The web-scale corpus likely contains the benchmark itself. Treat public-benchmark claims with suspicion; build private evals for anything you actually ship.

questions.q: Speculative decoding speeds up inference by:
opts: A small draft model proposing several tokens that the large model verifies in one parallel pass — output distribution provably unchanged
questions.expl: Verification accepts a run of draft tokens per big-model pass. Exactness is the beautiful part: rejection sampling preserves the target distribution.

questions.q: Weight-only quantization to int4:
opts: Cuts weight memory ~4× vs bf16 with modest quality loss — activations and KV cache are the harder parts to quantize
questions.expl: Weights tolerate low precision well (GPTQ/AWQ). The engineering fight moves to activation outliers and cache precision.

questions.q: vLLM's PagedAttention improves serving throughput by:
opts: Managing the KV cache in fixed-size pages (like virtual memory), eliminating fragmentation so far more concurrent sequences fit
questions.expl: Contiguous per-request cache allocation wastes memory on unpredictable lengths; paging packs it tight and shares prefixes.

questions.q: Why does LLM pretraining use learning-rate warmup?
opts: Adam's moment estimates are unreliable in the first steps and large early updates can destabilize training irreversibly
It increases the final learning rate
It only matters for small models
questions.expl: A few thousand gentle steps let optimizer statistics settle before full-size updates — cheap insurance against a run that never recovers.

questions.q: Neural scaling laws describe test loss as:
opts: A power law in model size, data, and compute — smooth, predictable improvement across orders of magnitude
questions.expl: Straight lines on log-log plots let labs forecast the value of compute before spending it — the discovery that turned scale into a strategy (and Chinchilla refined the recipe).
